{{smaller|English royal arms, notably in those of the present Prince of Wales.—'''Bend arrondi''', in ''her.'', a bend having one or both sides broken into concave curves. See ''gored''.—'''Bend cottised''', in ''her.'', a bend having on each side a cottise, separated from the bend by its own width. A bend may be double cottised or treble cottised; that is, it may have two or three cottises on each side.—'''Bend sinister''', in ''her.'' Same as ''bend'', 3, except that it is drawn from the sinister chief to the dexter base.}}

¶
'''bend<sup>3</sup>†''' (bend), ''n.'' [< late ME. ''bende'', < OF. ''bende'', var. of ''bande'', a band: see ''band''<sup>3</sup>.] An obsolete form of ''band''<sup>3</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>A fayre flocke of faeries, and a fresh ''bend''
Of lovely Nymphs. {{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., May.}}</poem>
The Duke of Gloucester . . . and other Lords, the chief of his ''bend.'' {{right|''Speed'', Hist. Gt. Brit., IX. xviii. 15.}}}}

'''bendable''' (ben′da-bl), ''a.'' [< ''bend''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] Capable of being bent; flexible. ''Sherwood.''

'''bende''' (bend), ''n.'' [Origin unknown.] A variety of the abelmoschus, used in cookery. ''McElrath.''

'''bendel†''', ''n.'' [ME., < OF. ''bendel'', ''bandel'', dim. of ''bende'', ''bande'', a band; doublet of ''bandel'', ''bandeau''.] '''1.''' A little band or fillet.—'''2.''' In ''her.'', a little bend.

'''bender''' (ben′dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who or that which bends.—'''2.''' A sixpence. [Eng. slang.]—'''3.''' A leg. [U. S. slang.]
{{smaller block|The prospectus [of a new fashionable boarding-school] has been sent to our house. One of the regulations is, “Young ladies are not allowed to cross their ''benders'' in school!” {{right|''Longfellow'', Kavanagh, xii.}}}}
'''4.''' A spree; a frolic. [U. S. slang.]—'''5.''' [Cf. ''bend''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 11.] A hard drinker. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Now lend your lungs, ye ''benders'' fine,
Wha ken the benefit of wine.
{{right|''Allan Ramsay'', Poems, III. 162 (1848).}}</poem>}}

¶
'''bending'''<sup>1</sup> (ben′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''bend''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] The act of causing to bend, or the state of being bent or deflected; a deflection.
{{smaller block|If matter that will not yield at each bend is deposited while the ''bendings'' are continually taking place, the ''bendings'' will maintain certain places of discontinuity in the deposit. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Biol., § 257.}}}}

'''bending'''<sup>2</sup>'''†''', ''n.'' [< ''bend''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', + ''-ing''.] Decoration (of clothes) with stripes or horizontal bands. ''Chaucer.''

'''bending-machine''' (ben′ding-mạ-shēn″), ''n.'' An apparatus for bending to shape timber, rails, iron beams for ships, plates for boilers, etc.

'''bending-strake''' (ben′ding-strāk), ''n.'' In ''ship-building'', one of two strakes wrought near the deck-coverings, worked all fore and aft. {{smaller|They are about an inch or an inch and a half thicker than the remainder of the deck, but are lowered between the beams and ledges to make the upper side even with the rest. Their use is to make a more complete tie between the deck-frame and deck-plank.}}

'''bend-leather''' (bend′leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' [< ''bend''<sup>1</sup> + ''leather''.] The strongest kind of sole-leather for shoes. See ''bend''<sup>2</sup>, 2.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bend|522|beneath}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Just ahead of us is a great ''bend'' in the river, beyond which the wind drops dead and the current hurls us up under a beetling crag.{{right|''C. W. Stoddard'', Mashallah, p. 137.}}}}
'''9.''' A curved or elbow-shaped pipe used to change direction, as in a drain.—'''10.''' A spring; a leap; a bound.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]—'''11.''' A “pull” of liquor.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Come, gie’s the other ''bend'',
We’ll drink their health, whatever way it end.</poem>{{right|''Allan Ramsay'', Gentle Shepherd, iii. 2.}}}}
'''12.''' In ''mining'', indurated clay, or any indurated argillaceous substance.—{{smaller|'''Close-return bend''', a short U-shaped tube joining the extremities of two wrought-iron pipes.—'''Grecian bend''', a mode of walking with a slight stoop forward, at one time affected by some women.}}

'''bend'''<sup>1</sup> (bend), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bent'', rarely ''bended'', ppr. ''bending''. [< ME. ''benden'', < AS. ''bendan'', bind, fetter, restrain, bend a bow (= MHG. ''benden'', fetter, = Icel. ''benda'' = Sw. ''bända'' = Dan. ''bænde'', bend; cf. OF. ''bender'', mod. F. ''bander'', tie, bind, bend, hoodwink, = Pr. ''bendar'' = Sp. Pg. ''vender'', bind, hoodwink, = It. ''bendare'', hoodwink), prop. fasten with a bend or band, < ''bend'', E. ''bend''<sup>1</sup>, a band, the noun being practically identical with ''band''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' The nouns and verbs of these groups (''band''<sup>1</sup>, ''bend''<sup>1</sup>, ''band''<sup>2</sup>, ''bend''<sup>2</sup>, etc.) reacted on each other both in Teut. and Rom., developing a variety of senses which have a double reference.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To bring or strain into a state of tension by curvature, as a bow preparatory to launching an arrow.
{{smaller block|What, are the hounds before and all the woodmen, Our horses ready and our bows ''bent?''
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Our English archers ''bent'' their bowes,
Their harts were good and trew;
Att the first flight of arrowes sent,
Full four-score Scots they slew.</poem>
{{right|''Percy’s Reliques'', p. 142.}}}}
Hence —'''2.''' Figuratively, to brace up or bring into tension, like a strong bow: generally with ''up''. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Now set the teeth, and stretch the nostril wide;
Hold hard the breath, and ''bend up'' every spirit
To his full height!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Her whole mind apparently ''bent up'' to the solemn interview.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii.}}}}
'''3.''' To curve or make crooked; deflect from a normal condition of straightness; flex: as, to ''bend'' a stick; to ''bend'' the arm.
{{smaller block|In duty ''bend'' thy knee to me.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A kindly old man, . . . somewhat ''bent'' by his legal erudition, as a shelf is by the weight of the books upon it.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Kavanagh, xvi.}}}}
'''4.''' To direct to a certain point: as, to ''bend'' one’s course, way, or steps; to ''bend'' one’s looks or eyes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Towards Coventry ''bend'' we our course.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Southwards, you may be sure, they ''bent'' their flight,
And harbour’d in a hollow rock at night.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, l. 1747.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How sweet are looks that ladies ''bend''
On whom their favors fall!</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Sir Galahad.}}}}
'''5.''' Figuratively, to apply closely: said of the mind. {{smaller block|It must needs be they should ''bend'' all their intentions and services to no other ends but to his.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|To ''bend'' his mind to any public business.
{{right|''Sir W. Temple.''}}}}
'''6.''' To incline; determine: said of a person or of his disposition: as, to be ''bent'' on mischief.
{{smaller block|Where will inclineth to goodnes, the mynde is ''bent'' to troth.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 79.}}}}
{{smaller block|One great design on which the king’s whole soul was ''bent''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Still ''bent'' to make some port he knows not where.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', A Summer Night.}}}}
'''7.''' To cause to bow or yield; subdue; make submissive: as, to ''bend'' a man to one’s will.
{{smaller block|<poem>Except she ''bend'' her humour.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh there are words and looks
To ''bend'' the sternest purpose!</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', The Cenci, v. 4.}}}}
'''8.''' ''Naut.'', to fasten by means of a bend or knot, as one rope to another, or to an anchor; to shackle, as a chain-cable to an anchor.—'''Bent lever, trimmer, graver''', {{smaller|etc. See the nouns.}}—'''To bend a sail''' {{smaller|(''naut.''), to make it fast to its proper yard, gaff, or stay, ready for setting.}}—'''To bend the brow''' {{smaller|or}} '''brows''', {{smaller|to knit the brow; scowl; frown.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be or become curved or crooked.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then was I as a tree
Whose boughs did ''bend'' with fruit.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' To incline; lean or turn; be directed: as, the road ''bends'' to the west.
{{smaller block|<poem>To whom our vows and wishes ''bend.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Arcades, l. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Our states daily
''Bending'' to bad, our hopes to worse.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Descend where alleys ''bend''
Into the sparry hollows of the world.</poem>
{{right|''Keats.''}}}}

'''3.''' To jut over; overhang.
{{smaller block|<poem>There is a cliff whose high and ''bending'' head
Looks fearfully in the confined deep.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 1.}}}}

'''4.''' To bow or be submissive: as, to ''bend'' to fate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Most humbly therefore ''bending'' to your state.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Must we ''bend'' to the artist, who considers us as nothing unless we are canvas or marble under his hands?
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Lit. Char. Men of Genius, p. 145.}}}}

'''5.''' To spring; bound.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]—'''6.''' To drink hard.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]—'''To bend to the oars''', {{smaller|to row vigorously.}}

'''bend<sup>2</sup>''' (bend), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bend'', ''bende'', partly < AS. ''bend'', a band used as an ornament (a sense of ''bend'', E. ''bend''<sup>1</sup>); partly < OF. ''bende'', mod. F. ''bande'' = Pr. ''benda'' = Sp. Pg. ''venda'' and ''banda'' = It. ''benda'', ''banda'', < ML. ''benda'', ''binda'', < OHG. ''binda'', a band, fillet, tie, mixed with ML. (etc.) ''banda'', < OHG. ''bend'', etc.: see ''band''<sup>2</sup>. ''Bend''<sup>2</sup> is thus in part historically identical with ''bend''<sup>1</sup>, but in part with ''band''<sup>2</sup>. The separation is now merely formal.]   '''1†.''' A band or strip used to bind around anything; a strip, whether as a fastening or as an ornament; a fillet, strap, bandage, etc.; specifically, a ribbon or bandeau for the head, used by ladies in the fifteenth century.
{{smaller block|<poem>And on her legs she painted buskins wore,
Basted with ''bends'' of gold on every side.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. v. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' A name in the leather trade for a butt or rounded crop cut in two; the half of a hide of sole-leather that was trimmed and divided before tanning.—'''3.''' In ''her.'', one of the nine ordinaries, consisting of a diagonal band drawn from the dexter chief to the sinister base: when charged, it occupies a third of the field; when uncharged, {{img float|file=century v01 p0548 c2f1.png|width=106px|align=left|cap={{smaller|A Bend azure.}}}} a fifth. {{smaller|Bearings are said to be ''in bend'' when they are placed upon the field obliquely in the direction of the bend; the field is said to be divided ''per bend'' when divided diagonally in that direction, usually by a straight line, but sometimes a broken line, battled, undé, or the like, or by a still more complicated mark of division. See ''bendwise.'' Also applied to a row of charges arranged in bend. ''In bend sinister'' and ''per bend sinister'' are used in a similar way.—'''Bend archy,''' in ''her.'', a band differing from the bend in that it is curved toward the sinister chief. Also called ''bend enarched'' or ''bowed.''—'''Bend archy, coronetty on the top,''' in ''her.'', a bend archy having the points or ornaments of a crown on the upper side. This is the well-known bearing of Saxony, which occurs in some English royal arms, notably in those of the present Prince of Wales.—'''Bend arrondi''', in ''her.'', a bend having one or both sides broken into concave curves. See ''gored''.—'''Bend cottised''', in ''her.'', a bend having on each side a cottise, separated from the bend by its own width. A bend may be double cottised or treble cottised; that is, it may have two or three cottises on each side.—'''Bend sinister''', in ''her.'' Same as ''bend'', 3, except that it is drawn from the sinister chief to the dexter base.}}

'''bend<sup>3</sup>†''' (bend), ''n.''   [< late ME. ''bende'', < OF. ''bende'', var. of ''bande'', a band: see ''band''<sup>3</sup>.]   An obsolete form of ''band''<sup>3</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>A fayre flocke of faeries, and a fresh ''bend''

{{smaller block|The prospectus [of a new fashionable boarding-school] has been sent to our house. One of the regulations is, “Young ladies are not allowed to cross their ''benders'' in school!” {{right|''Longfellow'', Kavanagh, xii.}}}}

'''Bendigo ware.''' See ''pottery.''

''beneden'' = LG. ''benedden'' = G. ''benieden''), < ''be'', by, + ''neothan'', ''nithan'', ''neothane'' (= OS. ''nithana'' = OHG. ''nidana'', MHG. ''nidene'', ''niden'', G. ''nieden''), below, orig., like ''nithe'', below, from compar. ''nither'', nether: see ''nether''. Hence by apheresis ''neath, ’neath.'']   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a lower place, position, or state, literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|Thou shalt be above only, and thou shalt not be ''beneath''.
{{right|Deut. xxviii. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Every brain
That looks so many fathoms to the sea,
And hears it roar ''beneath''. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4.}}

The general’s disdain’d
By him one step below; he, by the next;
